messages.subject: Parallelization in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Good morning!
I'm asking my university the access to a virtual machine with a lot of RAM and some parallel cpus.
My question is about the possibility to decrease computational time to run spatio-temporal models on big data sets: how many cpus should I ask for, based on the degree of parallelization of the software? Morover, is it useful to actually use more cpus in parallel or is it just a waste of computational power?
Thank you very much

messages.subject: Error message from using inla.tmarginal()
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Currently, I am trying to get the sample mean and standard deviation of a transformed parameter.

The parameter involved in the computation is the AR coefficient, rho, in the temporal latent effect 'ar1'. The transformed parameter theta = log((1+rho)/(1-rho)).

When I ran the following code
###################################################
## Transformation from (0,1) to (-Inf , Inf) with manual truncation
  to_normal = function(x){
    x_adj = ifelse(abs(x)>=.999999,sign(x)*.999999,x)
    return(log(1+x_adj)-log(1-x_adj))
  }
 inla_obj=inla(...) ## This is the inla model
### inla_obj$summary.hyperpar[[2]] is the corresponding rho from 'ar1'
 inla.zmarginal(inla.tmarginal(to_normal ,inla_obj$summary.hyperpar[[2]]),silent = TRUE)
####################################################

And I received the error message:
#########################################
Error in seq.default(xmin, xmax, len = n) :
  'from' must be a finite number
Calls: inla.tmarginal -> inla.smarginal -> seq -> seq.default
#########################################

It looks like some non-finite value is produced but I don't understand what is causing this issue. I've addressed the boundary issue by truncating the input before the transformation.

I really appreciate your help.

Best,
Yanzhao

messages.body_plain:
This is a very helpful thread.
I am fitting a similar model, but need to explore the temporally varying effect of a covariate. In this case, how should I revise the code? I used the f(index, covariate, ...) approach for besag, ar1 before for areal data, but not for geostatistical data using SPDE.

Thanks,

On Wednesday, June 22, 2022 at 12:19:22 AM UTC-7 eliask...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Tim,
>
> The example in the book works for spacetime varying regression coefficient. As you want the coefficient to vary only in space, you have to simplify things: the index set, the A matrix and the formula.
>
> i2 <- 1:spde$n.spde ### just spatial index
>
> A2 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = prmesh1, # SVC logw
>                       loc = cbind(dat$xcoo, dat$ycoo),
>                       weights = dat$logw)
> ### A2 = diag(covariate)  %*% A, each line (linked to one data point) of A is multiplied by the corresponding covariate value.
> f(i2, model = spde) ## the distribution for the random effect indexed by 'i2' is spatially structured
>
> Then this term in the linear predictor reads as
> ...  + u_i * covariate_i + ...
> where u_i = A_i * u_0, A_i being the usual projector matrix and u_0 the random field at the mesh nodes. Thus, the 'trick' is to pre-multiply A by the covariate so you don't need to have the covariate in the formula, as  f(index, covariate, ...) as in the other cases in INLA when you have other distributions for the coefficients (besag, ar, and such).
>
> best regards,
> Elias
>
>
> On Wed, 22 Jun 2022 at 01:38, Tim Meehan <tme...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Elias,
> >
> > Thanks for your initial response. After reading your message, I started to think of the model differently. Instead of calculating an SVC trend as part of the model, and then also trying to get the annual residual around the trend for annual abundance indices, I began thinking it is better to just use a spacetime model to get the abundance index across space per year, and then compute a trend from those estimates after modeling using the posteriors.

> > abundance index (per site and year) ~ zero centered IID site effect +
> >                                                                     SVC for count effort (per site) +

I tried using the weights argument to inla.spde.make.A() function to multiply A by the spatially varying covariate. But I get errors when trying to run inla() with this A matrix. > >                   sigma = sqrt(params[1]), n = k, mesh = prmesh1,
> >                   return.attributes = TRUE)
> > x <- x.k
> > for (j in 2:k) {x[, j] <- rho * x[, j - 1] + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * x.k[, j]}
> >
> > ## make covariate
> > n <- nrow(coords)
> > ccov <- factor(sample(LETTERS[1:3], n * k, replace = TRUE))
> > beta <- -1:1
> >
> > ## make response
> > sd.y <- 0.01
> > y <- beta[unclass(ccov)] + x + rnorm(n * k, 0, sd.y)
> >
> > ## package data
> > isel <- sample(1:(n * k), n * k / 2)
> > dat <- data.frame(y = as.vector(y), w = ccov,

> >                   ycoo = rep(coords[, 2], k))[isel, ]
> >
> > ##########################################################
> > # here i change the data to be more like the data i will be modeling.

> > dat$y <- round((dat$y^2), 0); summary(dat$y); hist(dat$y) # make it an integer count
> > dat$w <- as.numeric(dat$w); summary(dat$w); hist(dat$w) # make it a continuous cov
> > dat$logw <- log(dat$w)
> > dat$siteID <- as.integer(factor(paste(dat$ycoo, dat$xcoo)))
> > summary(dat)
> > ##########################################################
> >

> >                             prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)) # P(sigma > 1) = 0.01
> >
> > ###########################################################
> > # here i make two sets of indices because i hope to have the spacetime
> > # effect (intercept) and also a spatially varying coefficient for the covariate (logw)
> > iset <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde = spde$n.spde,
> >                              n.group = k) # space time intercept
> > iset2 <- inla.spde.make.index('i2', n.spde = spde$n.spde,
> >                              n.group = k) # SVC logw
> > ##########################################################
> >
> >
> > #########################################################
> > # here I make two sets of A matrices for the same reason as above.
> > # the second one for the SVC term has a weights argument so that
> > # the covariate is multiplied by the data projector matrix
> > A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = prmesh1, # space time intercept
> >                       loc = cbind(dat$xcoo, dat$ycoo), group = dat$time)
> > A2 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = prmesh1, # SVC logw
> >                       loc = cbind(dat$xcoo, dat$ycoo), group = dat$time,
> >                       weights = dat$logw)
> > #########################################################
> >
> > ## data stack
> > sdat <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(y = dat$y),
> >   A = list(A, A2, 1, 1),
> >   effects = list(iset, iset2,
> >                  logw = dat$logw,
> >                  siteID = dat$siteID),
> >   tag = 'stdata')
> >
> > ## priors
> > h.spec <- list(theta = list(prior = 'pccor1', param = c(0, 0.9)))
> > prec.prior <- list(prior = 'pc.prec', param = c(1, 0.01))
> >
> > ###########################################################
> > # this is the part that I can't get to work. when i try to get the spatially
> > # varying coefficient term in there, and then run the inla() function, i get an error:
> > # "There are one or more NA's in 'group' where 'idx' in f(idx,...) is not NA: # idx = 'i2'"
> > form <- y ~ 0 +
> >   f(siteID, model="iid", constr=T) + # random site effect
> >   f(i2, model = spde, # the problem term that is supposed to code the SVC
> >     group = i.group, control.group = list(model = 'ar1', hyper = h.spec)) +
> >   f(i, model = spde, # space time intercept
> >     group = i.group, control.group = list(model = 'ar1', hyper = h.spec))
> > ############################################################
> >
> > inla.setOption(inla.mode="experimental")
> > res <- inla(form,  data = inla.stack.data(sdat), family="nbinomial",
> >             control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE,
> >                                      A = inla.stack.A(sdat)),
> >             control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = prec.prior)),
> >             control.compute = list(waic = T, cpo = T,
> >                                    config = T),
> >             verbose = T,
> >             num.threads = 4,
> >             control.inla = list(strategy = 'adaptive', int.strategy = 'eb'))
> > summary(res)
> >
> > ## make plotting grid
> > stepsize <- 4 * 1 / 111
> > nxy <- round(c(diff(range(coords[, 1])),
> >                diff(range(coords[, 2]))) / stepsize)
> > projgrid <- inla.mesh.projector(
> >   prmesh1, xlim = range(coords[, 1]),
> >   ylim = range(coords[, 2]), dims = nxy)
> >
> > ## extract predictions
> > xmean <- list()
> > for (j in 1:k){
> >   xmean[[j]] <- inla.mesh.project(
> >     projgrid, res$summary.random$i$mean[iset$i.group == j])
> > }
> >
> > ## mask prediction grid
> > xy.in <http://xy.in> <- inout(projgrid$lattice$loc,
> >                cbind(PRborder[, 1], PRborder[, 2]))
> >
> > ## make a prediction raster stack and plot

> > invXtX <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X)

Any insights you can offer would be greatly appreciated!

Hanna

Hi,
This will depend on how you specify the model. E.g. if inla.stack is involved it’s safest to do the conversion to 0/1 variables yourself (with model.matrix) for full control.

I’m also not sure exactly what the ref argument actually does to the factor. If it reorders the levels to put the reference category as 1, it should be fine. If it just sets a flag for which level should be the reference, some code might not know how to deal with that.
I looks from the output that it has reordered the levels, so at least that part should be ok. What’s missing is just the removal of the reference category from the set of 0/1 variables. This is controlled by one of the inla arguments, and I know there can be an issue with that when using inla.stack, but it should otherwise be fine, so more details of your model specification are needed.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: Model selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yalem,

I'm not an expert. But hope this is helpful.

Best,
Tim

### From my reading and asking others:

## WAIC is 'better' than DIC. You get WAIC using the following.
# Theoretically, models that better balance prediction and parsimony (not overfit)
# have lower scores.
inla_waic <- inla_result$waic$waic

## Another model ranking criterion that reflects how the predictions match the
## data is the following.
# Better models have lower scores with this particular formulation. This score
# gets tricky when CPO is not well estimated, i.e., it fails the QC test or is NA.
cpo_vec <- inla_result$cpo$cpo
inla_bpic <- as.numeric(-2*sum(log(cpo_vec), na.rm=F))

# If that fails due to NA CPO values, try with the experimental version of INLA.
gcpo_vec <- inla_result$gcpo$gcpo
inla_bpic <- as.numeric(-2*sum(log(gcpo_vec), na.rm=F))

### Hopefully the two criteria above agree on a model. But also:

## Judge the fit of your model with the following.
# Libraries
library(inlatools)
library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)
library(dplyr)

# Diagnostic plots
dp1 <- dispersion_check(inla_result) %>% plot()
dp2 <- fast_distribution_check(inla_result) %>% plot()
dp3 <- ggplot(data.frame(x=inla_result$cpo$pit)) + geom_histogram(aes(x=x))
dp4 <- ggplot(data.frame(predicted=inla_result$summary.fitted.values$mean,
       observed=data_set$y), aes(x=observed, y=predicted)) +
       geom_hex() +
       geom_abline(aes(intercept=0, slope=1))
plot_grid(dp1, dp2, dp3, dp4)
# For dp3, ideally the histogram shows a uniform-ish distribution.
# For dp4, ideally the mass is along the 1:1 line.

# Hopefully there is a reasonable correlation between observed and mean predicted

messages.body_plain:
Check out the code below. If you are looking for something analogous to the "by"
argument in mgcv, try the "replicate" argument to inla that Finn mentioned. If you
are looking for something more like "fs" smooths in mgcv, try the "group"
argument in INLA. In both cases you get similar results with the two methods,
despite being quite different under the hood.

Best,
Tim

# libs
library(mgcv)
library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# data
d1 <- gamSim(eg=4, n=400, dist="normal", scale=2) %>%
  select(x2, fac, y) %>%
  mutate(x2_group=inla.group(x2), fac_idx=as.integer(fac)) %>%
  ungroup()

# gam with by
g1 <- gam(y ~ 1 + fac + s(x2, by=fac), data=d1)

# inla with replicate
i1 <- inla(y ~ 1 + fac + f(x2_group, model="rw2", replicate=fac_idx), data=d1)

# plot them, gam is dashed line
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=data.frame(fac=d1$fac, x2=d1$x2, pg=predict(g1)),
             aes(x=x2, y=pg, col=fac), lty=2, lwd=1) +
  geom_line(data=data.frame(fac=d1$fac, x2=d1$x2_group,
                        pi=i1$summary.fitted$mean),
                        aes(x=x2, y=pi, col=fac), lwd=1)

# gam with fs
g2 <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2, fac, bs="fs"), data=d1)

# inla with group
i2 <- inla(y ~ fac + f(x2_group, model="rw2", group=fac_idx,
                 control.group=list(model="iid")), data=d1)

# plot them, gam is dashed line
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=data.frame(fac=d1$fac, x2=d1$x2, pg=predict(g2)),
            aes(x=x2, y=pg, col=fac), lty=2, lwd=1) +
  geom_line(data=data.frame(fac=d1$fac, x2=d1$x2_group,
                            pi=i2$summary.fitted$mean),
            aes(x=x2, y=pi, col=fac), lwd=1)

messages.subject: 3-level model with temporal autocorrelation at one level
messages.subject_clean: 3-level model with temporal autocorrelation at one level
messages.body_plain:
Greetings list,

My data are annual measures of employees, and employees are nested within office locations. This can be thought of time (level 1) nested within employees (level 2), who are nested within offices (level 3).

I would like to specify a model with the repeated measures per employee with a random intercept that handles temporal autocorrelation (ar1 or rw1), and then have random intercepts for the offices. (The offices do not have spatial autcorrelation to worry about.)

How do I specify that?

mod1 <- inla(outcome ~ main_predictor + covariate + covariate_2 + ... +
                    f(employee_id, model = 'ar2') +
                    f(office_id, model = 'iid'))

But how does the inla know that employees are nested within office locations? mod1 would have two random effects, one for employees and one for offices. I would like the three-level hierarchy to be explicit.

Would this work?

mod2 <- inla(outcome ~ main_predictor + covariate + covariate_2 + ... +
                    f(employee_id, group = office_id, model = list('ar2', 'iid')))

  group_by() |>
  mutate(year = list(tibble(years = NA_integer_))) |>

dat

It occurred to me that simpler set up would be to use the sleepstudy data in lme4.

My intention is to articulate the questions better here.

library(tidyverse)
library(INLA)
library(lme4) # has sleepstudy data

data(sleepstudy)

# create a fake grouping of subjects
look_up <-
  tribble(
    ~'Subject', ~'Group',
    308, 'A',
    309, 'B',
    310, 'A',
    330, 'C',
    331, 'C',
    332, 'A',
    333, 'B',
    334, 'E',
    335, 'D',
    337, 'E',
    349, 'C',
    350, 'B',
    351, 'E',
    352, 'B',
    369, 'D',
    370, 'D',
    371, 'A',
    372, 'B') |>
  mutate(Subject = as.factor(Subject))

# add third-level group
(dat <- sleepstudy |> as_tibble() |> left_join(look_up, by = 'Subject'))

table(dat$Group)

# visualize set up
dat |>
  ggplot(aes(Days, Reaction)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(Group~Subject) +
  NULL

# frequentist model
mod_lmer   <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = dat)

# bayesian analogue with inla
mod_iid    <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, model = 'iid'), data = dat)

# similar estimates for both, successful double check
summary(mod_lmer)
mod_iid$summary.fixed

# suppose the data had a stronger temporal autocorrelation component, we could use
mod_ar1        <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, model = 'ar1'), data = dat) # or
mod_rw1        <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, model = 'rw1'), data = dat)

# instead of 'iid', great.

# but employees are now nested in Groups. The frequentist model could be
mod_lmer_3 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Group/Subject), data = dat)

# but lacks the desired correlation structure at the Subject level (like mod_ar1 and mod_rw1 above).
# Note that lmer complains about singularity

# Question 1: what is the inla equivalent? Something else?
mod_3a      <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject, group = Group, model = 'iid'))
mod_3b      <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Group, replicate = Subject, model = 'iid'))

# neither run.

# Question 2: how can that be extended to have ar1 within subjects and iid within groups?
mod_3_ar1_g  <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Subject
                                       , model = 'iid'
                                       , group = Group
                                       , control.group = list(model = 'ar1'))
                   , data = dat)

mod_3_ar1_r  <- inla(Reaction ~ Days + f(Group
                                       , model = 'ar1'
                                       , replicate = Subject
                                       )
                   , data = dat)

# end

Thank you for your consideration,
Dexter

messages.subject: Formulation of Knorr-Held models
messages.body_plain:
I wonder if someone could clarify the correct way to
set up Knorr-Held spatiotemporal models using
the group feature (and ignoring any identification
issues)? I've looked at two references:

B+C: Blangiardo and Cameletti, Spatio and Spatiotemporal
     Bayesian Modelling, section 7.1.2
R: Ravishanker et al, Dynamic Time Series Models, section 11.4

and they seem to do it differently for Types II and III.
In what I hope is an obvious abbreviated notation:

                          --------- R -------------                            ----------- B+C -------------
Type-II :  f(time/iid,   group=space/besag)   f(space/iid, group=time/rw2)
Type-III:  f(space/iid, group=time/rw1)         f(time/iid, group=space/besag)

They agree on Type-I (as you'd expect) and also on Type-IV.

I suppose that one possibility is that one of them has labelled as
Type-II what is actually Type-III, and vice versa. Another is that the
order doesn't matter and both are correct, (though I'd be a bit
surprised at this, given that we're aiming at a Kronecker product
model, where, as stressed by B+C, order does matter).

I'd be grateful for any help on this.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Fitting a spatial temporal SPDE model when data is not available for all years
messages.body_plain:
Hi McEwen,

yes, this is possible in principle. The details depend on what kind of
dependency model you want to have between the years.
You need to define your space-time model to include all the time
points that have observations as well as all the time points for which
you want to do prediction.
Whether those predictions are useful depends on how much information
there is about the temporal dependence in the data.

There are several options for spatio-temporal model; spatial field
plus spatially varying trend would be the simplest model, but could be
unrealistic.
A spatial model with an ar1 model as "group" model would be more flexible.
To make sure the model can be estimated, and since most of your data
is roughly equi-distant in time, I would suggest forst estimating the
model
using only the timepoints that have data (mapping 2000,2004,2010 and
2015 to 1, 2, 3, 4). That's less expensive to compute, and will show
if you have a model that at least fits the data you have, before
extending it to do interpolation/prediction.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] over-dispersed spatial counting data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The nbinomial and ZIP can be seen as two, different, extensions of a Poisson variable Y for a given lambda. However, if you use Poisson and consider lambda varying with some random effect and this random effect is at the level of each observation, this is better as you can check which observations have extra variability. This is towards trying to explain/model overdispersion directly instead of marginally doing with some Poisson extension to account for. Maybe the 'slm' model already explains the overdispersion and extending Poisson to nbinomial or ZIP does not add. Please consider a simpler example here: https://haakonbakkagit.github.io/btopic125.html

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject_clean: Excessive memory use for regression model
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to run a fairly complex linear regression model with many nested random intercepts and slopes and an autocorrelation term and a PC prior. I run this on different subsets of my data, which have between several 100 and 10.000 species (random effects) each, and each takes at least a day to run. But so far each model has crashed after at least 1 day of running, most with a Bus error, or an out or memory warning, and some don't specify.
